intro:
These exercises train one skill: looking at any line that reuses a value and naming exactly what happens to ownership there. A move hands a single value to a new owner. A copy is an implicit bitwise duplicate that small Copy types opt into. A clone is an explicit, possibly expensive duplication you write by hand. And a borrow avoids duplication entirely. The chapter's whole argument is that these are four different events with four different costs, and a reviewer should always be able to tell which one a given call site chose.

The set moves from classification to construction to judgment. You first label each event in a mixed flow and read a service path for its hidden allocation budget. Then you implement Clone by hand and strip clones that only existed to satisfy a too-greedy signature. The last two exercises are design calls: deciding when Copy is mechanically and semantically safe, and lining up receiver choice (self, &self, &mut self) with a deliberate duplication policy at a worker fan-out boundary. The lab closes the loop by making a manual Clone correct so that mutating a clone leaves the original untouched.

exerciseSolutions.title: Classify each duplication event correctly
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Walk each marked line and ask a single question: after this line runs, does the original binding still own its value, and if a duplicate exists, who paid for it and was it implicit or written down. That question separates the four events cleanly.

The move is the line that rebinds a non-Copy owned value, for example `let key = route_key;` where `route_key: String`. Ownership transfers to `key`, and `route_key` is no longer usable afterward. Nothing was duplicated; the single heap buffer simply changed owners. The implicit copy is the line that rebinds or passes a `Copy` value, for example `let id2 = id;` where `id: RequestId(u64)`. Because `RequestId` is `Copy`, the eight bytes are duplicated bitwise and `id` stays valid. There is no `.clone()` at the call site precisely because the duplication is trivial and the language makes it implicit.

The explicit clone is the line spelled `route.clone()` on a `String`, or `schema_string.clone()` on owned heap data. That call allocates a second independent buffer and copies the bytes, so later mutation of one does not touch the other. It is worth keeping the `Arc<Schema>` case distinct: `Arc::clone(&schema)` is also written explicitly, but it does not deep-copy the `Schema`. It adds a second owning handle to the same allocation and increments the strong count. Both handles see the same `Schema`; the clone is cheap because only a counter moved, not the payload.

The borrow is the line that takes `&value`, for example passing `&route` to a helper that only reads it. No ownership transfers and nothing is duplicated; the helper observes the existing value through a reference and the owner keeps it. That is the case where borrowing removes the need for duplication entirely: if the helper only inspects the route text, a `&str` argument means no clone and no move ever has to happen.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One flow showing a Copy, a move, an explicit Clone, an Arc share, and a borrow side by side.
criteria: Each event is named with the precise term move, copy, clone, or borrow rather than a vague 'copy-like' label.
Arc::clone is described as adding a shared owner and bumping the strong count, distinct from the deep String clone that allocates a new buffer.
The log_route(&owner) borrow is called out as the case where reading through a reference removes any need to move or clone.

exerciseSolutions.title: Find the hidden allocation budget
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Read the field types first; the cost of each duplication follows the ownership shape of the type, not the spelling of the operation. In a request path that duplicates a `RequestId`, clones a `String` route key, and clones an `Arc<Schema>`, the three operations have three different price tags.

Duplicating the `RequestId` is almost certainly trivial bitwise duplication. It wraps a `u64`, so it is `Copy`, and reusing it copies eight bytes on the stack with no allocation. Operationally, nothing touches the heap and the original `RequestId` stays valid. Cloning the `String` route key is the heap-backed operation: `String::clone` allocates a fresh buffer the size of the route text and memcpys the bytes into it, producing a second independent string. That is the line that actually spends from the allocation budget, and it spends every time the path runs.

Cloning the `Arc<Schema>` is neither of those. It increments an atomic reference count and returns a second handle pointing at the same `Schema` allocation. No `Schema` bytes are copied; the cost is one atomic increment, paid so the allocation lives until the last handle drops. Calling it a deep copy is the classic misread: the worker and the original share one `Schema`, they do not each own a private one.

The borrowing repair targets the `String` clone. If the helper that receives the route key only reads it, for example to log it or compare it, change its parameter to `&str` and pass `&route_key` instead of `route_key.clone()`. That removes the allocation entirely: the helper observes the existing buffer through a reference and the path keeps ownership. A cost review for this function should read: the `RequestId` reuse is a free scalar copy, the `Arc::clone` is one atomic increment for shared ownership, and the only real allocation is the `String` clone, which is removable by borrowing because the consumer is read-only.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: The route-key clone is the only line that allocates; audit_after shows the borrowing repair.
criteria: The RequestId reuse is identified as a trivial scalar Copy with no heap traffic.
The String route-key clone is identified as the heap-backed Clone that allocates a fresh buffer each call.
Arc::clone is explained as one atomic increment adding a shared owner, not a deep copy of the schema.
The proposed repair changes the read-only helper to take &str, removing the route-key allocation entirely.

exerciseSolutions.title: Implement Clone manually for a realistic type
exerciseSolutions.solution:
A correct manual `Clone` must produce a fully independent value: after cloning, mutating either the original or the clone must leave the other unchanged. For `JobTemplate { service: String, steps: Vec<String>, retries: usize }` that means each owned field has to be deep-cloned, and the scalar field is simply copied.

Clone the owned fields explicitly by calling `.clone()` on them. `self.service.clone()` allocates a new heap buffer for the service name; `self.steps.clone()` allocates a new `Vec` and clones each contained `String` into it. This is what guarantees independence: the clone's `steps` vector is a separate allocation, so pushing onto it later does not touch the original's vector. The `retries` field is a `usize`, a `Copy` scalar, so `retries: self.retries` copies the value directly. Writing `self.retries.clone()` would compile and behave identically because `usize: Clone`, but it adds nothing; copying the value is the idiomatic form.

The defect to avoid is exactly the one in the lab's starter code, which returns `String::new()` and `Vec::new()` for the owned fields. That is a stub, not a clone: it discards the data and produces an empty value that shares nothing with the original. The test for correctness is the mutation check. Clone, push a new step onto the clone's `steps`, and confirm the original's `steps.len()` is unchanged. A real clone passes this; the stub fails it because the original's data was never duplicated.

Keep the type non-`Copy`. `JobTemplate` owns heap memory through `String` and `Vec`, so it cannot be `Copy` mechanically, and even if it could, implicit duplication of a record that allocates would be misleading at call sites. `Clone` is the right trait here precisely because the cost is real and should be written down with an explicit `.clone()`.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Owned fields cloned explicitly, scalar copied directly; the assert proves clone independence.
criteria: Clone is implemented by hand in an impl block, not via a derive, placeholder, or stub.
service and steps are duplicated with .clone(), producing fresh heap allocations.
Pushing onto the clone's steps leaves the original's steps.len() at 2, proving independence.
The type stays non-Copy because it owns String and Vec heap data, where implicit duplication would mislead.

exerciseSolutions.title: Remove unnecessary clones from a read-only API
exerciseSolutions.solution:
The defect is a signature that takes ownership of data it only reads. `fn route_label(route: String) -> String` demands an owned `String`, so every caller that still needs its route afterward is forced to write `route_label(route.clone())` just to satisfy the parameter. The clone exists only to feed the signature, not because independent ownership is needed. The helper logs and compares route text; it never stores or mutates it.

The parameter should become `&str`. A read-only helper that inspects text needs nothing more than a borrowed view, and `&str` accepts both `&String` (via deref coercion) and string literals, so it is the most flexible read-only contract. The return type is the second decision. If the helper genuinely produces a new label, returning an owned `String` is honest. But if it returns the input unchanged in the common case, returning `Cow<'a, str>` lets the borrowed case avoid allocation and only the transformed case pay, matching the clone-on-write pattern the chapter uses. For a pure log-and-compare helper, the cleanest form often returns nothing or returns `&str` borrowed from the input, since no new owned string is created at all.

Once the parameter is `&str`, every `route_label(route.clone())` call site drops its `.clone()` and becomes `route_label(&route)`. The route stays owned by the caller, no allocation happens, and the same call works for literals too. One signature change removes clones at every call site at once, which is why fixing the parameter type is more valuable than patching individual callers.

Borrowing communicates the contract more clearly than taking ownership here. `fn route_label(route: String)` tells the reader the function might keep or consume the route, which is a lie for a helper that only reads. `fn route_label(route: &str)` states plainly that the function borrows and returns, makes no ownership claim, and lets the compiler guarantee the caller's value survives the call. The signature now documents the real behavior instead of forcing defensive clones.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Changing the parameter to &str drops the caller's clone; Cow allocates only on the rewrite branch.
criteria: The signature is changed to borrow with &str because read-only access is all the helper needs.
At least one caller drops its .clone(), passing &route instead.
The explanation states that &str documents the read-only, non-owning contract that String falsely implied.

exerciseSolutions.title: Decide whether a type should implement Copy
exerciseSolutions.solution:
`Copy` has two gates: a mechanical one the compiler enforces, and a semantic one you enforce in review. Mechanically, a type may be `Copy` only if it has no `Drop` implementation and every field is itself `Copy`. Semantically, it should be `Copy` only when an implicit bitwise duplicate is trivial and unsurprising, leaving both copies independently valid with no hidden cost or shared resource. The checklist is stricter than 'this seems lightweight.'

`RequestId(u64)` should be `Copy`. It wraps a single `u64`, which is `Copy`, it owns nothing on the heap, and duplicating an ID implicitly is exactly what callers expect. This is the canonical case for deriving `Copy, Clone`. `Span { start: usize, end: usize }` should also be `Copy`. Both fields are `Copy` scalars, the value is a plain pair of indices with no ownership, and an implicit duplicate of a span is predictable. Two small, trivially duplicable types, both safe.

`SessionKey(String)` must not be `Copy`, and the compiler will not allow it anyway because `String` owns heap memory and is not `Copy`. Even setting the mechanical rule aside, making session keys implicitly duplicable would hide allocations and blur the question of which copy is authoritative. It should be `Clone`, so duplication is explicit. `SocketOwner(TcpStream)` must not be `Copy` either. A `TcpStream` owns a file descriptor and has `Drop`, so the mechanical gate fails outright; semantically, two implicit owners of one socket is a correctness hazard. It should usually be neither `Copy` nor `Clone`. Resource ownership deserves a visible, deliberate API, often a move.

`SharedSchema(Arc<str>)` is the interesting one. `Arc<str>` is mechanically `Clone` but not `Copy`, so the wrapper cannot be `Copy` regardless. The temptation is that `Arc::clone` is cheap, so why not make the wrapper `Copy` to get implicit duplication. The answer: cheap to clone is not the same as trivial to copy. Each `Arc` clone performs an atomic reference-count increment, which has a real, if small, cost, and silently spawning shared owners on every implicit copy hides that the type participates in shared ownership. Keeping it `Clone`-only forces an explicit `.clone()` at each new owner, which is the visible signal shared ownership deserves. So: approve `Copy` for `RequestId` and `Span`; reject it for `SessionKey`, `SharedSchema`, and `SocketOwner`, using `Clone` for the first two and likely no duplication trait at all for the socket.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Copy for the trivial scalar wrappers; Clone for heap and shared owners; no trait for the socket.
criteria: Copy is approved only for RequestId and Span, where implicit duplication is trivial and unsurprising.
Copy is rejected for SessionKey (heap-owning) and SocketOwner (resource-owning with Drop).
The explanation states that Arc being cheap to clone does not justify Copy, because each clone is an atomic increment and shared ownership should be explicit.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose receivers and duplication boundaries together
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Receiver choice and duplication policy answer the same underlying question, which is who owns the value after a method runs, so design them together. The aim is that reading a method's receiver tells a reviewer the ownership transition, and every clone has a stated reason.

The builder's finalizer should consume `self`. `fn build(self) -> ServiceConfig` takes the builder by value because finalizing ends the builder's life: it converts accumulated state into the finished config and the builder should not be reusable afterward. Consuming `self` lets `build` move owned fields straight into the result with no clones, and the compiler enforces that no one keeps using the spent builder. During construction, the setter methods that only configure can take `&mut self` and return `&mut Self` for chaining, or take and return `self` if you prefer a move-based builder; either way they avoid rebuilding from a fresh clone on each step.

On the long-lived `ServiceConfig`, inspection methods take `&self`. `fn name(&self) -> &str` and `fn retries(&self) -> usize` borrow read-only and hand back a borrowed view or a copied scalar, so callers can query the config repeatedly without moving or cloning it. Mutations take `&mut self`. `fn bump_retries(&mut self)` edits in place rather than cloning the whole config, applying a change, and swapping it back, which would allocate a new config on every edit for no reason. The receiver set then reads as a contract: `&self` views, `&mut self` mutates in place, `self` finalizes or transforms ownership.

The `publish` fan-out is where an explicit clone or share is justified. If each worker needs its own independent, mutable copy of some job data, cloning per worker is legitimate: the clone buys independent ownership so workers do not contend, and you state that reason in review. But if the workers only read shared, immutable configuration, the right model is `Arc`: build one `Arc<ServiceConfig>` and hand each worker an `Arc::clone`, paying one atomic increment per worker instead of deep-copying the config N times. The tradeoff is concrete. Per-worker `Clone` costs N allocations and N deep copies but gives full independence; `Arc` costs N atomic increments and shares one allocation but forbids mutation without interior-mutability machinery. Choose `Clone` when workers must own and mutate, `Arc` when the data is genuinely read-shared, and avoid the two failure modes of cloning everything (wasted allocation) or forcing everything through `Arc` (atomic overhead and shared-state complexity where a plain move would do).
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: build(self) finalizes, &self/&mut self separate reads from edits, Arc shares one read-only config across workers.
criteria: build(self) consumes the builder to finalize, while &self inspects and &mut self mutates, so receivers express ownership transitions.
The Arc fan-out is justified economically: one allocation plus N atomic increments instead of N deep clones, chosen because workers only read.
The design avoids cloning everything and avoids forcing everything through Arc, picking each based on whether workers must own and mutate.
The tradeoff is named explicitly: per-worker Clone costs allocations for independence, Arc costs atomic increments for shared read-only access.

labSolution.explanation:
The starter code's manual Clone is a stub: it returns String::new() and Vec::new() for the owned fields, discarding the original's data. The fix is to deep-clone each owned field with self.service.clone() and self.steps.clone(), and to copy the scalar retries directly with self.retries. This is exactly what #[derive(Clone)] would generate; writing it by hand makes the duplication of each field explicit.

Because steps is cloned into a fresh Vec backed by its own allocation, the clone is independent of the original. When main pushes "notify" onto cloned.steps, only the clone's vector grows. The original still owns its two-element vector, untouched.

That independence is what produces the expected output. The first line reads original.service ("billing") and original.steps.len() (still 2), printing 'original = billing 2'. The second reads the clone, whose steps now holds three entries after the push, printing 'cloned = billing 3'. The clone's service is its own "billing" buffer copied from the original. The third line prints the copied scalar, 'retries = 2'.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between moving a `String`, copying a `u64`, and cloning an `Arc<T>`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Moving a String transfers ownership of its single heap buffer to a new binding and invalidates the old one, so no data is duplicated and the original can no longer be used. Copying a u64 is an implicit bitwise duplicate of eight stack bytes that leaves the original valid, because u64 is Copy and the duplication is trivial. Cloning an Arc<T> creates a second owning handle to the same allocation by incrementing an atomic reference count; it does not duplicate the inner T, it adds a shared owner so the value lives until the last handle drops.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `Copy` intentionally much narrower than 'cheap enough to duplicate'?
reviewAnswers.answer: Copy makes duplication implicit, so the language will silently duplicate the value on assignment and argument passing while keeping the original valid; that is only safe when the duplicate is a trivial bitwise copy with no hidden cost and no shared resource. Mechanically Rust forbids Copy on any type with a Drop impl or a non-Copy field, which rules out heap owners, file descriptors, and reference-counted handles. Even types that are cheap to clone, like an Arc wrapper, are deliberately excluded, because an Arc clone is an atomic increment that participates in shared ownership and should be written down explicitly rather than happening invisibly.

reviewAnswers.question: When is `Cow<'a, str>` a better API than always returning `String`?
reviewAnswers.answer: Cow<'a, str> is better when the common case returns the input unchanged and only some inputs require a rewrite. The borrowed branch (Cow::Borrowed) returns a reference with no allocation, and the owned branch (Cow::Owned) allocates only when the value is actually transformed, so the API pays for an owned String exactly when one is needed. Always returning String forces an allocation on every call even when the input was already in the right form, which wastes work on the hot path of unchanged inputs.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is `Arc::clone` not the same thing as deep-cloning the inner value?
reviewAnswers.answer: Arc::clone copies only the handle, not the payload: it increments the strong reference count and returns a second Arc pointing at the same allocation, so both handles observe one shared inner value. A deep clone of the inner value would allocate a separate copy that the two owners could mutate independently. With Arc the value is shared, not duplicated, which is what makes the clone cheap (one atomic increment) and also why mistaking it for a deep copy leads to wrong reasoning about how many independent copies exist.

reviewAnswers.question: How do receiver choices reduce unnecessary cloning in production APIs?
reviewAnswers.answer: Choosing &self for read-only methods lets callers inspect a value repeatedly without moving or cloning it, since the method borrows rather than taking ownership. Choosing &mut self lets a method edit a value in place instead of cloning it, mutating a copy, and swapping it back. Reserving self for finalizers and transforms lets those methods move owned fields straight out with no clone. Together these receivers express the real ownership contract, so callers are not pushed into defensive clones just to satisfy a signature that demanded more ownership than the method actually needed.
